avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous paddy monocropping depletes soil nitrogen and builds up rice-specific pests/diseases (e.g., stem borer, blast).
rationale: Rice is a nitrogen-exhaustive, non-leguminous cereal. Rotating with a nitrogen-fixing legume restores soil nitrogen via Rhizobium symbiosis, improving the following cereal's yield. Rice-pulse rotation is a standard recommended practice in Indian rice-based cropping systems (ICAR).

avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous maize cultivation allows maize-specific pests (stem borer, fall armyworm) to build up in the soil and residue.
rationale: Maize is a nitrogen-exhaustive cereal. Summer-legume-to-maize sequences are a well-studied ICAR cropping pattern that improves soil nitrogen status and reduces fertilizer dependency for the following maize crop.

avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous cotton cultivation causes severe bollworm (Helicoverpa) buildup and heavily depletes soil nitrogen and micronutrients.
rationale: Cotton is an exhaustive, non-leguminous crop. Cotton-to-Bengal gram (chickpea) is a classic, widely documented Indian rotation used specifically to restore soil fertility and break the cotton pest cycle.

avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous jute cultivation depletes soil nitrogen and potassium and increases root-rot pathogen buildup.
rationale: Jute is a nitrogen-exhaustive fibre crop, commonly grown in eastern India in sequence with pulses. Following it with a legume restores soil nitrogen ahead of the next fibre or cereal season.

avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous chickpea cultivation builds up Fusarium wilt (a major soil-borne chickpea disease) and pod-borer (Helicoverpa) populations.
rationale: Chickpea fixes atmospheric nitrogen via Rhizobium and is best followed by a nitrogen-demanding cereal or cash crop to make use of the residual soil nitrogen, per standard legume-cereal sequencing (ICAR).

avoid_repeat_reason: Repeated kidney bean cultivation increases root-rot and bean common mosaic virus incidence.
rationale: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, kidney beans (rajma) enrich the soil for a following cereal crop, consistent with the general legume-to-cereal rotation principle.

avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous pigeon pea cultivation increases Fusarium wilt and pod-borer (Helicoverpa) buildup.
rationale: Pigeon pea (arhar/tur) is a deep-rooted nitrogen-fixing legume commonly rotated ahead of cereals and cotton to restore soil nitrogen and break pest cycles specific to continuous cropping.

avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous moth bean cultivation increases yellow mosaic virus incidence, common across Vigna-family pulses.
rationale: As a Vigna-family nitrogen-fixing legume adapted to arid conditions, moth bean follows the same legume-to-cereal rotation logic used for other pulses.

avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous mungbean cultivation increases yellow mosaic virus and Cercospora leaf-spot incidence.
rationale: Mungbean (green gram) is a fast-growing nitrogen-fixing legume frequently used as a summer catch crop ahead of maize or rice to improve soil nitrogen status (ICAR summer-legume-maize studies).

avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous blackgram cultivation increases yellow mosaic virus and root-knot nematode incidence.
rationale: Blackgram (urad) is a nitrogen-fixing legume commonly grown in rotation with rice in eastern and southern India, restoring soil nitrogen for the following cereal season.

avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous lentil cultivation increases Fusarium wilt and rust incidence.
rationale: Lentil (masoor) is a nitrogen-fixing rabi-season legume typically rotated with a cereal, consistent with standard legume-cereal sequencing to restore soil nitrogen.

avoid_repeat_reason: Repeated cucurbit cultivation on the same plot builds up Fusarium wilt and fruit-fly populations specific to the cucurbit family.
rationale: Cucurbits are prone to soil-borne wilt pathogens and fruit-fly buildup when repeatedly grown on the same land; rotating out of the cucurbit family (into legumes or cereals) is standard practice to break the disease/pest cycle.

avoid_repeat_reason: Repeated cucurbit cultivation on the same plot builds up Fusarium wilt and fruit-fly populations specific to the cucurbit family.
rationale: Same cucurbit-family disease/pest dynamics as watermelon; rotating into a legume or cereal breaks the cycle and, if a legume is chosen, adds a nitrogen benefit.

Mango is a multi-decade perennial tree crop. Single-season crop rotation logic does not apply. Intercropping with short-duration legumes during the tree's juvenile (non-bearing) years is a separate agronomic practice, not modeled here.
Coconut palms remain productive for 60+ years. Rotation logic does not apply; intercropping (e.g., with cocoa, pepper, or fodder) is a distinct practice not modeled in this rotation matrix.
Coffee is a multi-year perennial shrub crop grown under shade plantations. Seasonal rotation is not applicable.
Apple is a temperate perennial fruit tree with a multi-decade orchard lifecycle. Rotation logic does not apply.
Orange (citrus) is a perennial orchard tree crop with a multi-decade lifecycle. Rotation logic does not apply.
Grapevines are perennial and remain productive for 20-25+ years on a trellis system. Rotation logic does not apply.

Banana is a long-duration (12+ month) perennial-type crop typically maintained across multiple ratoon cycles on the same plot. Classic single-season rotation logic does not apply; replanting decisions depend on ratoon management practice, not modeled here.
Papaya is typically maintained as a 2-3 year orchard crop rather than a single-season crop. Classic annual rotation logic does not apply.
Pomegranate is a perennial orchard shrub with a multi-decade productive lifespan. Rotation logic does not apply.

avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous soybean cultivation increases the risk of root rot and other soil-borne diseases.
rationale: Soybean is a nitrogen-fixing legume, highly recommended after cereals and avoids repeat due to root rot.
Bajra (pearl millet) is a nitrogen-exhaustive cereal/millet, typically recommended after pulses like chickpea or mungbean.

avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous jowar cultivation depletes soil nitrogen.
rationale: Jowar (sorghum) is a nitrogen-exhaustive cereal, commonly recommended after pulses to utilize fixed nitrogen.

avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous groundnut cultivation increases incidence of soil-borne diseases and pests.
rationale: Groundnut is an oilseed legume that fixes nitrogen, making it ideal before nitrogen-demanding cereals or cotton.

avoid_repeat_reason: Continuous sugarcane monocropping severely depletes soil nutrients and increases pest buildup.
rationale: Sugarcane is a long-duration cash crop that depletes nitrogen. It is recommended to rotate with pulses or fallow to restore soil health.
